name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,308

entries.clue: Dad’s good-humoured joking — something useful on his travels (8)

blocks.note: sport = fun, jesting, as in 'said in sport'

annotation.surface: A father's cheerful banter keeps the family going on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash seems to explain Dad's jokes as the useful thing; in fact it separates wordplay from definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A passport is the document every traveller needs.

entries.clue: Put forward non-poetic writing — Romeo no longer features (4)

indicators.note: Romeo stops appearing in the word, so R is taken out

blocks.note: prose is writing that is not verse
Romeo = R in the NATO alphabet; removed

annotation.surface: An editor proposes cutting Shakespeare's Romeo from a prose adaptation.
annotation.walkthrough: PROSE without its R leaves POSE, as in 'pose a question'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: raising a question or problem for others to consider.

entries.clue: One demonstrating, saying little, a popular bathroom feature? (6,7)

blocks.note: a show-er, one who shows; read it to rhyme with 'grower'

annotation.surface: A laconic salesman shows off a fashionable fitting in a bathroom showroom.
annotation.walkthrough: SHOWER is two words in one: the person who shows, and the thing you stand under. The clue uses the first and the answer the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A shower curtain hangs around the shower in many bathrooms.

entries.clue: Men unpaid — mob almost involved in uproar (11)

indicators.note: mob falls one letter short, losing its B
letters that are involved are tangled up together, so they lose their order

annotation.surface: Workers left without wages are joined by a crowd, and a riot breaks out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'involved in uproar' one phrase about the mob; split it so 'in' merely links the wordplay to 'uproar'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym; Milton coined the word for the capital of Hell, a place of all demons, hence wild noisy chaos.

entries.clue: Break in secluded place (6)

blocks.note: a pause in business, as when a parliament or school stops sitting
a nook or alcove set back out of sight, as in the hidden corners of a house

annotation.surface: Someone takes a breather in a quiet corner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Break in' reads as burglary, but 'in' is only the join between two meanings of one word.
annotation.definitionFit: Recess covers both a pause in proceedings and an alcove or remote spot.

entries.clue: Drink, quiet, for those left (4)

annotation.surface: A quiet drink is poured in memory of the departed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Those left' sounds like mourners or leftovers; a rump is the small remnant of a larger body, as in the Rump Parliament.
annotation.definitionFit: The rump of a group is the remnant that remains after the rest have gone.

entries.clue: New, excited punter needed calming at first (13)

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters are stirred into a new order
take only the opening letter of 'calming'

annotation.surface: A worked-up gambler at the racecourse needs settling down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New, excited' looks like two adjectives for the punter; 'New' alone is the definition. A punter is a bettor.
annotation.definitionFit: Something unprecedented has never happened before, so it is new.

entries.clue: No self-reliant type — operating as pirate (8)

indicators.note: operating means working on something, and here the letters are worked into a new order

annotation.surface: A freeloader is accused of acting like a buccaneer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Operating' reads as the pirate going about his work; it is the instruction to rework the eight letters of 'as pirate'.
annotation.definitionFit: A parasite lives off others rather than supporting itself.

entries.clue: Disdain introduction of some banal material (5)

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A critic sneers at a preface full of clichés.
annotation.walkthrough: Corn is used for anything trite or sentimental, the root of 'corny'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words, as noun or verb, name contempt for something thought worthless.

entries.clue: Maybe Ivy’s more weird after one’s left (7)

indicators.note: one (I) has departed from the word

blocks.note: one = I, the Roman numeral; removed

annotation.surface: Ivy, the person, seems stranger once somebody has walked out.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on Ivy makes it look like a name; it is the plant, and 'Maybe' flags it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'Maybe': ivy is one of many climbing plants.

entries.clue: Nice, clear it’s changing, light’s better, thanks to him? (11)

indicators.note: letters that are changing alter their arrangement

annotation.surface: Someone admires how bright a room is after a bulb was changed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Changing' belongs with the light bulb in the surface; here it rearranges the letters before it. The question mark marks a definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: An electrician fixes the wiring, so the lighting improves thanks to him.

entries.clue: Dancing events seen (about five) with little between contestants (4,7)

indicators.note: letters that are dancing move around the floor, so they will not stay in the order given
the fodder goes around V, so V joins the mix

annotation.surface: A spectator at a dance competition finds the couples barely separated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Even stevens' is informal for level, all square.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: rhyming informal slang meaning level, with neither side ahead.

entries.clue: Study sea’s unusual weekly occurrences (8)

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement is not the ordinary one, so the letters are reordered

annotation.surface: A marine biologist examines odd events on the ocean.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', a join, and adds no S to the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Tuesdays come round once every week.

entries.clue: Out of fashion, a French firm, old, ultimately eliminated (6)

annotation.surface: An outdated French company is finally wound up.
annotation.walkthrough: Un is the French indefinite article, and firm gives CO because Co. abbreviates company.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something uncool is out of step with current fashion.

entries.clue: Initially attempt to buy energy supplies tested under most favourable conditions (2,4)

indicators.note: take the initial letter of each following word

blocks.clueFragment: attempt to buy energy supplies tested
blocks.note: first letters of Attempt To Buy Energy Supplies Tested

annotation.surface: A company tries to purchase power that has already been proved reliable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initially' governs every word from 'attempt' to 'tested', not just the first; the surface hides six initials in a sentence about an energy deal.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'at best' qualifies a statement as holding only in the most favourable case.

entries.clue: Something maybe written on back of envelope in Land’s End erroneously? (6)

definitions.text: Something maybe written on back of envelope

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: A letter goes astray because it was addressed wrongly to Land's End.
annotation.walkthrough: Land's End is the far south-west tip of England. The sender's name and address is often written on the back flap of an envelope.
annotation.definitionFit: The sender's details are what is often written on the back of an envelope.

entries.clue: Feature of court’s employment policy (7,4)

blocks.note: service = employment, as in 'in his service'
line = policy, as in 'the party line'

annotation.surface: A law court's staffing rules are under review.
annotation.walkthrough: The court sounds legal or royal; it is a tennis court.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: the marking on a tennis court that bounds where a serve must land.

entries.clue: Beastly sound? Daughter’s temper (4)

annotation.surface: A parent hears a growl and knows the daughter is in a bad temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' suggests something nasty; it just means made by a beast.
annotation.definitionFit: A temper is a mood, as in 'in a good temper'.

entries.clue: Worried — a learner, ready to fight? (7)

annotation.surface: A nervous novice squares up for a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: L for learner comes from the L-plate a British learner driver must display.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe someone made anxious by a threat.

entries.clue: Train trouble — just a bit for a start (5)

indicators.note: only a fragment of the preceding words is used

annotation.surface: A commuter shrugs off a minor rail delay at the start of the journey.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Just a bit' reads as minimising the trouble; it tells you to take a small piece of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: A clipped informal form: short for introduction, the opening of a song, talk or book.

entries.clue: Unhappy about northern beach feature (4)

indicators.note: about means around, so SAD is placed around the N

annotation.surface: A gloomy stretch of coast in the north.
annotation.walkthrough: Northern gives N, the standard compass abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the most familiar thing a beach is made of.

entries.clue: Unwind regularly, welcomed by group of three in island (8)

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of 'unwind' is taken
the group of three takes the letters in

blocks.note: a triad is a group of three; the outside
uNwInD, the even letters; the inside

annotation.surface: A trio of holidaymakers relaxes on a Caribbean island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In island' looks like the setting of the scene; 'in' only links the wordplay to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a Caribbean island, the larger of the pair that makes one nation with Tobago.
